request: We'd like managers to edit and re-approve documents after they've already been signed.

problem.value: Managers need a way to correct or update documents that have already been signed, likely because errors are found or terms change after signature — but the underlying trigger (correction vs. renegotiation vs. periodic update) is not stated.
problem.evidence: "edit and re-approve documents after they've already been signed"

current_process.evidence: Not mentioned — unclear whether today this is handled outside the system (manual re-signature, new document altogether) or not handled at all.

actors.value: "Managers" are named as the actor who edits and re-approves, but it's unclear if they are the original signatories/approvers or a distinct role with override authority.

business_objects.value: Document, Version, Approval/Signatory are the objects in play, per the platform's core model.
business_objects.evidence: Context: Document vs Version distinction, Approval circuit.

business_rules.value: Unclear whether re-approval after edit requires the full original approval circuit, a lighter single-manager approval, or a rule that varies by document type/classification.
business_rules.evidence: Context: "the identity of the re-approver after an edit is rarely the same as the original"; request only says 'managers... re-approve' without specifying circuit.

workflow.value: Likely: editing a signed document should create a new version (supersession), with the prior signed version retained and referenceable, rather than an in-place edit — this is the platform's standard pattern but not confirmed by the client.
workflow.evidence: Context: "a later edit is a new version, never an in-place change... the prior version is retained and stays referenceable."

integrations.evidence: Not stated — who/what should be notified when a document is re-edited and re-approved is unspecified.

permissions.value: Unclear whether all managers can edit any signed document, or only those tied to their scope/classification/original ownership.
permissions.evidence: Context: "who can see it is driven by classification... reclassifying is high-blast-radius"; request doesn't specify scope of manager authority.

config_vs_custom.value: Approval circuits and classification schemes are client-specific; whether the re-approval rule after edit is standard-for-all or configurable per client is unresolved.

constraints.value: Editing a signed document raises legal/e-signature validity questions: are prior signatures invalidated, must they be re-collected, and does this interact with retention/legal-hold rules?
constraints.evidence: Context: "prior signatures invalidated or re-collected"; "electronic-signature validity" listed as a regulatory sensitivity.

edge_cases.evidence: Not addressed: what if the document is already published/distributed when edited? What if under legal hold? Concurrent edits by two managers?

reporting.value: An audit trail of who edited, who re-approved, when, and why is expected given the compliance nature of signed documents — not explicitly requested but implied by the domain.
reporting.evidence: Context: "an audit trail... is a hard requirement, not a nice-to-have."

risks.value: Risk that re-editing signed documents undermines the legal defensibility of the signature/approval trail if not carefully scoped and audited.
risks.evidence: Context: retention/legal-hold and e-signature validity sensitivities.

questions.q: When a manager edits a signed document, should this always create a new version — keeping the previously signed version intact and referenceable — rather than modifying the signed content in place?
questions.why: uncertainty × impact: this is the core blind spot — 'edit a signed document' almost always means supersession, not an in-place change, and it determines the whole data/versioning model.

questions.q: After an edit, must the document go back through the full original approval circuit (all approvers again), or can a manager alone re-approve it? Does this depend on the type or classification of the document?
questions.why: uncertainty × impact: determines whether this is a simple manager override or a full circuit re-trigger — directly shapes approval logic and effort.

questions.q: Are 'managers' here the same people as the original approvers/signatories, or a separate role allowed to override any signed document regardless of who approved it originally?
questions.why: uncertainty × impact: defines the authorization boundary; getting this wrong risks managers editing documents outside their proper scope.

questions.q: Once a document is edited and re-approved, are the original signatures considered invalidated (must be re-collected), or does the new version simply become current while the old one remains a valid historical record?
questions.why: uncertainty × impact: touches e-signature legal validity — a wrong assumption here creates compliance exposure.

questions.q: Do you need a visible audit trail (who edited, who re-approved, when, and why) accessible to compliance/records officers for every re-approved document?
questions.why: uncertainty × impact: signed/approved documents are typically compliance-sensitive; an audit trail is a different build than a simple edit log and is expensive to retrofit.

summary.objective: Allow managers to modify a document that has already been signed and put it through re-approval, while preserving the integrity and traceability of the original signed record.
summary.scope: Likely involves: creating a new version upon edit (supersession) rather than mutating the signed version, defining a re-approval path (full circuit vs. lightweight manager approval), scoping who may trigger this (permissions), handling the fate of prior signatures, and logging the change for audit purposes.
assumptions: Editing a signed document should produce a new version, retaining the old signed version as a historical record (standard platform pattern).
Managers requesting this capability are presumably tied to or overriding the original approval circuit, though this is unconfirmed.
An audit trail of edits and re-approvals is required given the compliance-sensitive nature of signed documents.
The re-approval likely needs to be a defined circuit (not ad hoc), consistent with existing approval-circuit patterns in the platform.
summary.blind_spot: The request describes the desired action ('edit and re-approve') but not what happens to the previously signed version and its legal status — without clarifying whether this creates a new version (supersession) with the old one retained, and whether prior signatures are invalidated or preserved, the team risks building a simple in-place edit that breaks signature integrity and audit defensibility.

business_objects.evidence: Context: 'content immutability after approval... a later edit is a new version, never an in-place change.'

workflow.value: Likely: signed version → manager edits → new draft version → re-review/re-approval → new version becomes current; original retained. Exact transitions and whether publication status is affected mid-flight are unconfirmed.
workflow.evidence: Context: two independent lifecycles (approval vs publication) plus supersession pattern.

questions.q: While the edited version is pending re-approval, should the previously signed/published version remain the 'current' one people act on, or should it be withdrawn immediately?
questions.why: uncertainty × impact: conflates the approval and publication lifecycles — a wrong default could let people act on a stale or a not-yet-valid version.

questions.q: Is a full audit trail (previous content, new content, who edited, who re-approved, when) required for compliance, and should it be visible to a compliance/records officer role?
questions.why: uncertainty × impact: compliance/audit needs named in the domain make this high-impact; retrofitting an audit trail later is expensive.

summary.scope: Likely scope: on edit, create a new Version of the Document (original signed version retained and referenceable); route the new version through a re-approval step (same or adapted circuit); manage which version is 'current' for readers during the pending re-approval window; log the change for audit purposes.
assumptions: Editing produces a new version rather than mutating the signed content in place.

An audit trail of edits and re-approvals is expected given the compliance-sensitive domain.

summary.objective: Allow managers to modify a document that has already been signed/approved, and put it back through approval — without breaking the integrity of what was previously signed.
summary.scope: Likely involves: creating a new version when a signed document is edited (rather than mutating it in place), re-triggering the approval/signature circuit on that new version, deciding what happens to the old signed version and its visibility, and logging the whole change for auditability. Very possibly touches the existing approval-circuit engine and the publication/current-version logic already built.
assumptions: The underlying need is to correct or update signed documents without restarting the whole document from scratch.
Editing produces a new version while the original signed version is retained as a historical record (supersession pattern), not an in-place overwrite.
Managers here means a specific role with document-edit rights, not any manager platform-wide.
Original signatures are invalidated by the edit and must be re-collected on the new version.

summary.blind_spot: The request reads as a small UX ask ('let managers edit and re-approve'), but it actually hinges on the supersession model: what happens to the original signed content, whether prior signatures are still valid, who can see which version during the pending re-approval window, and whether the same approval circuit applies. Building this as a simple in-place edit would silently break signature validity and version integrity — the exact trap this platform's domain notes warn about.

briefs.problem: There is no sanctioned way to correct a signed document without either mutating a legally-signed record or starting over with a brand-new document.
briefs.solution: An edit-and-re-approval workflow for signed documents that creates a new version, retains the original, and re-runs some form of approval.
introduces: a supersession/versioning engine specifically for already-signed content
a re-approval circuit that may differ in shape and reviewers from the original approval
classification- or ownership-scoped permission logic for who may trigger an edit
an audit trail linking edit → re-approval → new version, for compliance defensibility
handling of prior-signature status (invalidated vs. preserved) with e-signature legal implications
notification routing for re-approval events across roles

challenges.headline: Any manager can edit any signed document
challenges.premise: The request treats 'managers' as a single authorized group able to edit and re-approve signed documents.
challenges.alternative: Scoping edit rights to the document's classification, its original approval circuit, or the manager's ownership of it keeps override authority proportionate to the document's sensitivity, the same way classification already drives read access.
challenges.consequence: A blanket manager-edit right on signed, potentially legally binding documents is a governance gap that will surface at acceptance testing or, worse, in an audit.
challenges.recommendation: Define the authorization boundary (role, ownership, classification) before building the edit trigger, not after.

challenges.headline: Single flat re-approval step
challenges.premise: The request implies 're-approve' is one uniform action regardless of document type.
challenges.alternative: Tying the re-approval shape to document classification or type — full circuit re-run for contracts or regulated documents, a lighter single sign-off for low-risk internal ones — matches effort to actual risk instead of a one-size rule.
challenges.consequence: A flat rule either over-engineers trivial edits or under-protects documents that legally need every original signatory's consent again.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client whether re-approval circuit composition varies by document type/classification before designing the workflow states.

challenges.headline: Fate of prior signatures left implicit
challenges.premise: The request assumes editing and re-approving 'just works' without addressing what happens to the original signatures.
challenges.alternative: Explicitly deciding — as a legal/compliance question, not a technical default — whether prior signatures are invalidated and must be re-collected, or remain valid against the old version while only the new version needs fresh approval, protects the platform's signature validity claims.
challenges.consequence: Leaving this implicit risks a version that looks approved but whose legal signature chain doesn't actually cover its content — a defensibility problem discovered only when challenged.
challenges.recommendation: Get this ruling from legal/compliance before the workflow states are finalized.

complexity_reasons: versioning/supersession logic layered on top of an existing approval circuit
re-approval rules likely vary by classification or document type
audit trail must cover edit, re-approval and version linkage with no gaps
signature validity handling has legal exposure if the rule is wrong
briefs.cost_driver: the re-approval circuit logic and its interaction with versioning (deciding and building full-circuit vs. lightweight re-approval by document type)
risks: Building a simple in-place edit instead of proper supersession would break signature integrity and audit defensibility.
The existing approval-circuit engine assumes a single lifecycle; extending it for a distinct re-approval identity (per context: 'the re-approver is rarely the same as the original') is nontrivial.
Two managers editing the same signed document concurrently is unaddressed and will surface as a data-integrity bug if not designed for.
If editing can also touch classification, the change ripples into search, listings, notifications and export per the platform's existing cross-cutting access model.
Retrofitting the audit trail after the fact is expensive — it needs to be part of the initial design, not bolted on.

opportunities.text: Model this as the platform's general supersession pattern (frozen version → new version, old retained and referenceable) rather than a one-off feature specific to this request.
Extend the existing approval-circuit engine to support a distinct 're-approval' circuit definition (different reviewers, different quorum) rather than hardcoding a second approval path.
The audit trail built for edit/re-approval traceability is the same shape needed for other compliance-sensitive change logs across the platform.

next_steps: Confirm with the client that editing a signed document always creates a new version, with the signed original retained and referenceable, before designing the data model.

Settle whether re-approval circuit composition is fixed, or varies by document type/classification, and who exactly is authorized to trigger an edit.
Specify the audit trail and notification requirements (who is told an edit/re-approval happened, and on which event) before implementation starts.

briefs.problem: Managers have no sanctioned way to fix a signed-off document without breaking its frozen, legally-signed state or restarting the whole approval process from scratch.
briefs.solution: A version-supersession flow: editing a signed document creates a new version that goes through re-approval, while the original signed version is retained and referenceable.
introduces: a version-supersession engine distinct from a simple edit form
a re-approval routing path that may or may not reuse the original signing circuit
an explicit 'current version' resolution rule for the window while re-approval is pending
signature re-validation or re-collection logic tied to e-signature law
an audit trail surface covering edit, approval and version-supersession events

challenges.headline: Re-approval assumed to bypass original signatories
challenges.premise: The request frames this as 'managers edit and re-approve,' implicitly treating re-approval as a managerial formality rather than a re-run of the original signing.
challenges.alternative: Route the new version through the same approval circuit and signatories as the original document, with 'manager' only as the trigger for edit, not as a substitute approver.
challenges.consequence: If any manager can re-approve regardless of who signed originally, the reissued document may carry legal weight it hasn't actually earned, and the original signatories lose control over content they were accountable for.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with legal/compliance whether re-approval must involve the original signatories, and whether it must be a re-signature, not just a sign-off click.

challenges.headline: Signature invalidation left unresolved
challenges.premise: The request talks about 're-approving' a document, without addressing what happens to the legal validity of the prior signatures once content changes.
challenges.alternative: Treat any edit to signed content as invalidating prior signatures outright, forcing a full re-signature cycle rather than a lighter re-approval step, since e-signature validity is tied to the exact content signed.
challenges.consequence: Shipping a 're-approve' flow that doesn't formally invalidate/re-collect signatures risks producing a document that is operationally 'approved' but legally unenforceable.
challenges.recommendation: Get an explicit ruling from whoever owns e-signature compliance before designing the re-approval step.

challenges.headline: 'Current' version during pending re-approval
challenges.premise: The workflow assumes a clean handoff from signed version to new version, but doesn't say what readers see while the edited version is still awaiting re-approval.
challenges.alternative: Keep the previously signed/published version as 'current' and visibly mark the edited version as 'pending re-approval,' rather than letting the edit silently become the acting document before it's approved.
challenges.consequence: Without an explicit rule, either readers keep acting on a version the manager considers outdated, or they start acting on unapproved content — both are exactly the failure mode the platform's approved-vs-published distinction exists to prevent.
challenges.recommendation: Define the interim state and its visibility before building the version-switch logic.

Build the edit/re-approval audit trail on the same auditable-change pattern needed for regulatory reporting elsewhere in the platform, rather than a document-specific log.

decisions.decision: Editing a signed document produces a new Version rather than mutating the signed content in place; the original is retained and stays referenceable.

decisions.alternative: Allow direct in-place editing of the signed content.
decisions.tradeoff: Added versioning and supersession complexity, in exchange for not breaking signature validity and audit integrity.

decisions.decision: An audit trail covering the edit, the new version's content, and the re-approval will be required given the domain's compliance posture.

challenges.headline: Edit framed as overwrite, not supersession
challenges.premise: The request says managers 'edit and re-approve' a signed document, which reads like modifying the existing record in place.
challenges.alternative: Treat every edit to a signed document as a new version: the prior signed content is frozen and retained, the edit becomes a fresh version that re-enters approval on its own.
challenges.consequence: Building this as an in-place edit silently invalidates prior signatures, breaks anything referencing the old content, and removes the very audit trail the platform's compliance posture depends on.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client that supersession — not overwrite — is the model, before any schema or workflow work starts.

challenges.headline: Same approval circuit assumed for re-approval
challenges.premise: The request implies the edited document simply goes back through approval, without saying whether it's the identical circuit (same approvers, same quorum) as the original signature.
challenges.alternative: A lighter or differently-scoped circuit for edits (e.g. only the original approver, or a role tied to the document's classification) keeps minor corrections from carrying the full original sign-off overhead, while major changes still get full re-approval.
challenges.consequence: Forcing every edit through the full original circuit regardless of materiality will make managers avoid using the feature, or push them back to 'start a new document' — defeating the point of building it.
challenges.recommendation: Ask whether re-approval should vary by edit type or document classification before designing the circuit re-trigger.

challenges.headline: Blanket 'managers can edit' rights
challenges.premise: The request names 'managers' as the actor who can edit and re-approve, without scoping which managers or tying it to document ownership.
challenges.alternative: Scope edit rights to the document owner, a role tied to the document's classification, or an explicit list of eligible editors — consistent with how classification already drives visibility on this platform.
challenges.consequence: An undefined 'any manager' right conflicts with the classification-based access model already in place and is the kind of gap that surfaces at acceptance testing, not before.
challenges.recommendation: Define the eligible-editor role precisely, and check whether it should vary by document classification.

Once the supersession pattern is generalized here, it can also cover legal-hold interactions (blocking edits or re-approval on documents frozen by a hold) without a separate build.

open_decisions: Does 'edit' mean supersession (new version, old retained) or an in-place overwrite?
Does re-approval reuse the exact original circuit, or a lighter/different one, and does that vary by document type or classification?
Who exactly counts as an eligible 'manager' — any manager, the document owner, or a classification-tied role?
Are original signatures invalidated and re-collected on the new version, or retained as historical?
What stays visible to readers while a new version is pending re-approval — the old signed version, the pending one, both, or neither?
Is this behaviour standard across all document types/classifications, or configurable per client?
What audit trail detail (who, what, when, why) is required, and is it exportable for compliance review?
How are concurrent edits by two managers on the same document handled?
